_readme: Curated company events for the Stock Journey timeline.
THIS FILE IS DATA, NOT CODE. Adding events, companies or whole categories is an
edit here plus a `build_db.py` run -- no application logic changes. `build_db`
validates every row against the contract below and refuses to build on a bad one,
because a silently dropped event looks identical to a company that simply has none.
Event contract (all fields required, all strings):
symbol      a ticker present in data/symbols.csv
date        ISO YYYY-MM-DD. The date the MARKET could act on the news -- the
session the chart actually turns, not the internal decision date.
Split dates are the first split-adjusted trading day for the same
reason: that is the row a reader sees.
title       short label for the timeline marker (aim for <= 40 chars)
description one or two sentences that TEACH. The marker says what; this says
why it mattered. Never restate the price move -- that is computed
from the data and shown beside it.
category    a name listed in `categories` below
source      provenance for the claim, so a later editor can re-verify it
Events dated before a symbol's first price row (the dataset starts ~2001) are kept
deliberately: they never draw a marker, but they are true facts about the company
and they feed the Did You Know panel. `JOURNEY_COMPANY_EVENTS` filters by date.
Quality bar: verifiable, dated, and consequential. A press release is not an event.
Absent is better than approximate -- a wrong date puts a marker on the wrong crater.

events.title: Apple goes public
events.description: Apple sold 4.6 million shares at $22 in the largest IPO since Ford in 1956, creating roughly 300 millionaires on the first day.
events.source: Apple Computer Inc. 1980 prospectus; SEC EDGAR CIK 0000320193

events.title: iPod introduced
events.description: A 5GB music player with 'a thousand songs in your pocket'. It began Apple's shift from a computer maker into a consumer devices company.

events.title: 2-for-1 stock split
events.description: Apple's third split, after the iPod had roughly tripled the share price in a year.

events.title: iPhone unveiled
events.description: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone at Macworld and dropped 'Computer' from the company name the same day. The product went on to supply the majority of Apple's revenue.

events.title: iPad goes on sale
events.description: Apple created the modern tablet category and sold a million units in under a month.

events.title: Tim Cook becomes CEO
events.description: Steve Jobs resigned as chief executive on health grounds and was succeeded by his operations chief. Cook had already run the company during three medical leaves.

events.title: Steve Jobs dies
events.description: Apple's co-founder died at 56, the day after the iPhone 4S launch he did not appear at.

events.title: 7-for-1 stock split
events.description: An unusually large ratio, taking the share price from roughly $650 to $93 and making Apple eligible for the price-weighted Dow, which added it a year earlier than it otherwise could have.

events.title: First $1 trillion company
events.description: Apple became the first US public company to close above a $1tn market value, 38 years after its IPO.

events.title: 4-for-1 stock split
events.description: Apple's fifth split, executed while the stock was compounding through the pandemic recovery.

events.title: Vision Pro announced
events.description: Apple's first new computing category since the Apple Watch, and its most expensive consumer product at $3,499.

events.title: Microsoft goes public
events.description: Shares priced at $21. A $1,000 stake held through all nine subsequent splits became one of the best-known compounding stories in US equities.

events.title: First-ever dividend declared
events.description: After 17 years of retaining every dollar, Microsoft began returning cash — an admission that the hyper-growth phase had ended.

events.title: 2-for-1 stock split
events.description: Microsoft's ninth and, to date, final stock split.

events.title: Skype acquired for $8.5bn
events.description: Microsoft's largest acquisition at the time. It was written down almost entirely within a decade.

events.title: Satya Nadella becomes CEO
events.description: The third CEO in Microsoft's history pivoted the company to cloud and subscriptions, ending the Windows-first strategy.

events.title: LinkedIn acquisition closes
events.description: A $26.2bn deal, then Microsoft's largest, bringing a professional social graph alongside Office.

events.title: GitHub acquisition closes
events.description: $7.5bn in stock for the world's largest code host — a reversal for a company whose CEO had once called open source a cancer.

events.title: Crosses $1 trillion
events.description: Microsoft closed above a $1tn valuation for the first time, on Azure growth rather than Windows.

events.title: Multiyear OpenAI investment
events.description: Microsoft confirmed a reported $10bn extension of its OpenAI partnership, making Azure the exclusive cloud for the most visible AI lab.

events.title: Activision Blizzard closes
events.description: $68.7bn, the largest acquisition in gaming history, after a 21-month fight with UK and US regulators.

events.title: NVIDIA goes public
events.description: Priced at $12 a share as a graphics-chip maker for PC gaming, two decades before the AI cycle it would come to define.
events.source: NVIDIA Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001045810

events.title: CUDA announced
events.description: A programming model that let general-purpose code run on graphics hardware. It turned a gaming chip into a scientific computing platform and became NVIDIA's deepest moat.

events.title: Mellanox acquisition closes
events.description: $6.9bn for high-speed interconnect. Data-centre AI clusters are limited by networking as much as by compute, and this bought the networking.

events.title: 4-for-1 stock split
events.description: The first split since 2007, after the stock had roughly quadrupled in two years.

events.title: Arm acquisition abandoned
events.description: NVIDIA walked away from a $40bn deal for Arm under regulatory opposition on three continents — the largest semiconductor deal never completed.

events.title: AI guidance shocks the market
events.description: NVIDIA guided to quarterly revenue roughly 50% above consensus on data-centre demand. It was the moment the AI buildout showed up in a public company's numbers.

events.title: Crosses $1 trillion
events.description: NVIDIA touched a $1tn market value intraday, the first chipmaker to do so.

events.title: 10-for-1 stock split
events.description: A second split in three years, after the AI cycle took the share price above $1,200.

events.title: Most valuable company in the world
events.description: NVIDIA passed Microsoft and Apple to become the largest US public company by market value.

events.title: Avago Technologies IPO
events.description: The former HP/Agilent semiconductor unit went public at $15 after a private-equity carve-out. It later bought Broadcom and took its name.

events.title: Broadcom merger completes
events.description: Avago paid $37bn for Broadcom and adopted the name — the largest semiconductor deal to that point, and the template for a decade of roll-ups.

events.title: Qualcomm bid blocked
events.description: A presidential order blocked Broadcom's $117bn hostile bid on national-security grounds, ending the largest attempted tech acquisition ever.

events.title: VMware acquisition closes
events.description: $69bn in cash and stock, pushing Broadcom decisively into enterprise software alongside its chip business.

events.title: 10-for-1 stock split
events.description: Broadcom's first split, after AI networking demand took the share price above $1,700.

events.title: Oracle goes public
events.description: Priced at $15 one day before Microsoft's IPO, on revenue of $55m.

events.title: PeopleSoft acquired for $10.3bn
events.description: The end of an 18-month hostile pursuit that PeopleSoft's board fought publicly. It began Oracle's decade of consolidating enterprise software.

events.title: Sun Microsystems acquired
events.description: $7.4bn brought Oracle into hardware and handed it Java and MySQL — assets that shaped a decade of licensing litigation.

events.title: Larry Ellison steps down as CEO
events.description: Oracle's co-founder moved to CTO and chairman after 37 years, with Safra Catz and Mark Hurd named co-CEOs.

events.title: NetSuite acquisition closes
events.description: $9.3bn for a cloud ERP business Ellison had personally seeded, accelerating Oracle's move off on-premise licences.

events.title: Salesforce goes public
events.description: Priced at $11 on the argument that business software would be rented, not installed — the thesis that defined SaaS.

events.title: MuleSoft acquisition closes
events.description: $6.5bn for integration software, Salesforce's largest deal to that point.

events.title: Tableau acquisition closes
events.description: $15.7bn in stock for analytics and visualization, immediately doubling Salesforce's largest-deal record.

events.title: Joins the Dow Jones
events.description: Salesforce replaced Exxon Mobil in the Dow on the same day — a clean marker of the index's rotation from energy to software.
events.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices announcement, 24 Aug 2020

events.title: Slack acquisition closes
events.description: $27.7bn, Salesforce's largest acquisition, bought to contest Microsoft Teams at the centre of workplace software.

events.title: ATI acquisition closes
events.description: $5.4bn for the graphics maker. The debt from this deal nearly ended AMD, and the technology eventually became its console and datacentre business.

events.title: GlobalFoundries spun out
events.description: AMD sold its factories and became a fabless designer — a forced restructuring that later proved to be the right structure.

events.title: Lisa Su becomes CEO
events.description: Su took over a company trading near $3 with declining share in every market it served, and led one of the largest turnarounds in semiconductor history.

events.title: Ryzen launches
events.description: The Zen architecture made AMD competitive with Intel on desktop performance for the first time in a decade.

events.title: Xilinx acquisition closes
events.description: $49bn in stock for programmable chips — an all-stock deal made possible by the share price Ryzen and EPYC had rebuilt.

events.title: Macromedia acquisition closes
events.description: $3.4bn brought Flash, Dreamweaver and Fireworks under one roof and removed Adobe's closest competitor in creative tools.

events.title: Creative Suite goes subscription-only
events.description: Adobe stopped selling perpetual licences entirely. Revenue fell for two years before the recurring model produced a far larger business.

events.title: $20bn Figma deal announced
events.description: Adobe agreed to pay roughly 50x annual recurring revenue for a design tool that was taking its market. Investors treated the price as an admission of weakness.

events.title: Figma deal abandoned
events.description: Adobe and Figma terminated the deal under UK and EU opposition, and Adobe paid a $1bn break fee.

events.title: Most valuable company in the world
events.description: Cisco passed Microsoft at roughly $555bn at the peak of the dot-com bubble. It has never regained that valuation.

events.title: Scientific Atlanta acquired
events.description: $6.9bn for set-top boxes, a bet that video traffic would drive network demand.

events.title: Consumer business shut down
events.description: Cisco killed the Flip camcorder and retreated from consumer products, cutting 550 jobs and refocusing on enterprise networking.

events.title: Chuck Robbins becomes CEO
events.description: John Chambers stepped down after 20 years, handing over a company shifting from hardware boxes to software and subscriptions.

events.title: Splunk acquisition closes
events.description: $28bn for security and observability software, Cisco's largest deal ever and its clearest move away from hardware.

events.title: Brian Krzanich becomes CEO
events.description: Intel promoted its manufacturing chief as the company was missing the shift to mobile entirely.

events.title: CEO resigns over relationship
events.description: Krzanich left after an investigation found a past consensual relationship with an employee, breaching Intel's non-fraternization policy.

events.title: 7nm delay disclosed
events.description: Intel said its next process node had slipped roughly a year. The manufacturing lead it had held since the 1990s was publicly gone.

events.title: Pat Gelsinger becomes CEO
events.description: A former Intel CTO returned from VMware promising to rebuild leading-edge manufacturing and open a foundry business.

events.title: Dividend suspended, 15% of staff cut
events.description: Intel halted a dividend it had paid since 1992 and announced roughly 15,000 job cuts alongside a large earnings miss.

events.title: Gelsinger departs abruptly
events.description: Intel announced its CEO had retired effective immediately, four years into a turnaround plan the board had run out of patience for.

events.title: Apple sues over licensing
events.description: Apple filed a $1bn suit challenging Qualcomm's practice of charging royalties as a percentage of the whole device price, opening a two-year global fight.
events.source: Apple Inc. v. Qualcomm Inc., S.D. Cal., 20 Jan 2017

events.title: NXP acquisition abandoned
events.description: Qualcomm walked away from a $44bn deal after Chinese approval never arrived, and paid a $2bn break fee.

events.title: Apple settlement
events.description: Apple and Qualcomm settled all litigation worldwide mid-trial, with a payment to Qualcomm and a six-year supply agreement. Intel exited the 5G modem business the same day.

events.title: National Semiconductor acquired
events.description: $6.5bn for analog chips, consolidating TI's position in the least cyclical, highest-margin corner of semiconductors.

events.title: Haviv Ilan named president
events.description: Part of a planned succession that made Ilan CEO in 2023, as TI committed to a decade-long domestic 300mm fab buildout.

events.title: PwC Consulting acquired
events.description: $3.5bn for 30,000 consultants, the deal that turned IBM from a hardware company into a services company.

events.title: PC business sold to Lenovo
events.description: IBM exited the business it had invented in 1981 for $1.75bn, judging personal computers permanently unprofitable at scale.

events.title: Watson wins Jeopardy!
events.description: IBM's question-answering system beat the game's two best human players, and became the brand IBM attached to a decade of AI positioning.

events.title: Ginni Rometty becomes CEO
events.description: IBM's first female chief executive inherited a company whose revenue would decline for most of her tenure.

events.title: Red Hat acquisition closes
events.description: $34bn, IBM's largest deal ever, buying the leading enterprise Linux and Kubernetes vendor to compete in hybrid cloud.

events.title: Arvind Krishna becomes CEO
events.description: The architect of the Red Hat deal took over, and moved quickly to shed the legacy infrastructure services business.

events.title: Kyndryl spun off
events.description: IBM separated $19bn of managed infrastructure revenue into a new public company, shrinking itself deliberately to raise its growth rate.

events.title: Google goes public
events.description: A $85 Dutch-auction IPO designed to bypass Wall Street allocation, with a dual-class structure that kept founder control — a template much of tech later copied.
events.source: Google Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001288776

events.title: YouTube acquisition closes
events.description: $1.65bn in stock for a 20-month-old site with no revenue and serious copyright exposure. It became one of the best-returning acquisitions ever made.

events.title: First Android phone announced
events.description: The T-Mobile G1 shipped the operating system that now runs the majority of the world's smartphones and protects Google's search distribution.

events.title: Class C share split
events.description: A 2-for-1 split creating non-voting Class C stock, cementing founder control while still issuing equity.

events.title: Alphabet restructuring completes
events.description: Google became a subsidiary of a new holding company, separating the profitable search business from the loss-making 'Other Bets'.

events.title: Sundar Pichai becomes Alphabet CEO
events.description: Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped back from day-to-day roles, consolidating Google and Alphabet leadership under one executive.

events.title: 20-for-1 stock split
events.description: Alphabet's first split in eight years, bringing the share price from roughly $2,200 down to about $110.

events.title: Bard demo error
events.description: Alphabet's answer to ChatGPT gave a factually wrong answer in its own launch advertisement, feeding a narrative that Google was losing the AI lead.

events.title: First dividend declared
events.description: Alphabet announced its first-ever dividend alongside a $70bn buyback, 20 years after listing.

events.title: Facebook goes public
events.description: A $104bn debut marred by Nasdaq system failures. The stock fell more than 50% within four months as investors doubted it could monetize mobile.
events.source: Facebook Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001326801

events.title: Instagram acquisition closes
events.description: About $1bn for a 13-person company with no revenue — later regarded as one of the most valuable acquisitions in corporate history.

events.title: WhatsApp acquisition closes
events.description: $19bn for a messaging app with 55 employees, securing Facebook's position in mobile communication outside the US.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica scandal breaks
events.description: Reporting that data on tens of millions of users reached a political consultancy triggered congressional hearings, a record FTC fine and permanent changes to platform data access.

events.title: Largest one-day loss in US history
events.description: Facebook shed roughly $119bn of market value in a session after warning that revenue growth would decelerate for years.

events.title: Renamed Meta Platforms
events.description: Facebook renamed itself around the metaverse and began disclosing Reality Labs separately, revealing losses above $10bn a year.

events.title: First-ever daily user decline
events.description: Meta reported falling daily users and quantified Apple's privacy changes at roughly $10bn of 2022 revenue.

events.title: 'Year of Efficiency' declared
events.description: Meta paired deep cost cuts with a large buyback after a 64% drawdown, and the stock more than doubled over the following year.

events.title: First dividend declared
events.description: Meta initiated a dividend and added $50bn to buybacks, completing its transition from growth story to cash-return story.

events.title: Netflix goes public
events.description: Priced at $15 as a DVD-by-mail service with 600,000 subscribers.
events.source: Netflix Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001065280

events.title: Streaming launches
events.description: Netflix began delivering video over the internet as a free add-on to DVD subscriptions, cannibalizing its own profitable business on purpose.

events.title: Qwikster splits the service
events.description: A price rise and a plan to separate DVDs into a new brand cost Netflix 800,000 subscribers. Qwikster was cancelled within a month; the stock fell roughly 75% over the period.

events.title: House of Cards premieres
events.description: Netflix released a full season of an original series at once, establishing both binge-release and the streaming original.

events.title: 7-for-1 stock split
events.description: Netflix's second split, after streaming growth took the share price above $700.

events.title: First subscriber loss in a decade
events.description: Netflix lost 200,000 subscribers and guided to a much larger decline, ending the growth-at-any-price framing that had supported its multiple.

events.title: Ad-supported tier launches
events.description: Netflix reversed a long-held position against advertising, opening a second revenue stream after subscriber growth stalled.

events.title: US password-sharing crackdown
events.description: Netflix began charging for out-of-household accounts in its largest market. Widely predicted to cause cancellations, it produced the strongest additions in years.

events.title: Bob Iger becomes CEO
events.description: Iger succeeded Michael Eisner after a shareholder revolt, and immediately repaired the relationship with Pixar that Eisner had broken.

events.title: Pixar acquisition closes
events.description: $7.4bn in stock. It made Steve Jobs Disney's largest individual shareholder and put Pixar's leadership in charge of Disney Animation.

events.title: Marvel acquisition closes
events.description: $4bn for a character library that went on to produce the highest-grossing film franchise in history.

events.title: Lucasfilm acquisition closes
events.description: $4.05bn for Star Wars and Indiana Jones, completing Disney's roll-up of the largest franchises in film.

events.title: 21st Century Fox acquisition closes
events.description: $71bn for Fox's entertainment assets, bought to supply a streaming service and to take control of Hulu.

events.title: Disney+ launches
events.description: The service reached 10 million sign-ups on day one, and Disney began pulling its films back from Netflix.

events.title: Bob Iger returns as CEO
events.description: Disney's board removed Bob Chapek and brought Iger back after streaming losses and a collapsing share price.

events.title: SBC buys AT&T and takes its name
events.description: A former regional Bell bought its old parent for $16bn and adopted the AT&T brand, largely reassembling the company broken up in 1984.

events.title: T-Mobile deal abandoned
events.description: AT&T dropped a $39bn acquisition under DOJ and FCC opposition, and paid a $4bn break-up package — one of the largest ever.

events.title: DirecTV acquisition closes
events.description: $48.5bn for satellite television, at what proved to be the peak of the pay-TV subscriber base.

events.title: Time Warner acquisition closes
events.description: $85bn after AT&T defeated the DOJ in court. The combined debt load exceeded $180bn and constrained the company for years.

events.title: WarnerMedia spun off, dividend cut
events.description: AT&T unwound the media strategy within four years, spinning WarnerMedia into Warner Bros. Discovery and cutting its dividend by roughly 45%.

events.title: Buys out Vodafone's stake
events.description: $130bn — one of the largest corporate transactions ever — gave Verizon full ownership of its own wireless business.

events.title: AOL acquisition closes
events.description: $4.4bn, the first half of a digital advertising strategy meant to reduce dependence on wireless subscriptions.

events.title: Yahoo acquisition closes
events.description: $4.48bn, cut by $350m after two enormous breach disclosures during due diligence.

events.title: Verizon Media sold to Apollo
events.description: Verizon sold AOL and Yahoo for $5bn, abandoning the advertising strategy at a large loss.

events.title: Amazon goes public
events.description: Priced at $18 as an online bookseller with $16m of annual revenue and no profits — a condition it maintained deliberately for two decades.
events.source: Amazon.com Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001018724

events.title: Prime launches
events.description: $79 a year for unlimited two-day shipping. Internally expected to be unprofitable, it became the mechanism that locked in customer spend.

events.title: AWS launches with S3
events.description: Amazon began renting infrastructure to other companies. AWS now supplies the majority of Amazon's operating profit.

events.title: Kindle launches
events.description: Amazon attacked its own founding business with a dedicated e-reader; the first run sold out in hours.

events.title: Whole Foods acquisition closes
events.description: $13.7bn for 460 physical stores. Grocery and pharmacy stocks fell sharply on the announcement across the sector.

events.title: Crosses $1 trillion intraday
events.description: Amazon became the second US company to reach a $1tn valuation, a month after Apple.

events.title: Andy Jassy becomes CEO
events.description: Jeff Bezos moved to executive chairman after 27 years, handing over to the executive who had built AWS.

events.title: 20-for-1 stock split
events.description: Amazon's first split since 1999, taking the share price from roughly $2,400 to about $120.

events.title: Tesla goes public
events.description: Priced at $17, the first American car maker to list since Ford in 1956, with cumulative losses and one low-volume model.
events.source: Tesla Motors Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001318605

events.title: Model S deliveries begin
events.description: The car that established Tesla as a real manufacturer rather than a niche converter of other companies' chassis.

events.title: Model 3 deliveries begin
events.description: Tesla's mass-market car, followed by the 'production hell' period in which the company came close to running out of cash.

events.title: 'Funding secured' tweet
events.description: Elon Musk tweeted about taking Tesla private at $420. The SEC charged him with fraud; he paid $20m and gave up the chairmanship.
events.source: SEC v. Elon Musk, S.D.N.Y., 27 Sep 2018

events.title: 5-for-1 stock split
events.description: Tesla's first split, after the stock had risen roughly 500% in a year.

events.title: Joins the S&P 500
events.description: Added at roughly $650bn, the largest company ever admitted to the index, forcing index funds into a single enormous purchase.
events.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices announcement, 16 Nov 2020

events.title: Crosses $1 trillion
events.description: A 100,000-vehicle order from Hertz took Tesla past a $1tn valuation, above the next several car makers combined.

events.title: 3-for-1 stock split
events.description: Tesla's second split in two years.

events.title: Bob Nardelli becomes CEO
events.description: A GE executive brought centralization and cost discipline to a decentralized retailer; sales rose while the share price went nowhere for six years.

events.title: Nardelli ousted
events.description: Home Depot's board removed Nardelli after a shareholder revolt over pay, with a severance package near $210m.

events.title: Payment data breach disclosed
events.description: Home Depot confirmed a breach affecting 56 million payment cards, then the largest retail card breach on record.

events.title: First quarterly loss ever
events.description: McDonald's reported a loss for Q4 2002, its first as a public company, after years of over-expansion and declining store quality.

events.title: Chipotle fully divested
events.description: McDonald's completed its exit from Chipotle after the 2006 IPO, giving up one of the best-performing restaurant stocks of the following decade.

events.title: Steve Easterbrook becomes CEO
events.description: Easterbrook took over amid falling US traffic and launched all-day breakfast and the refranchising program.

events.title: Easterbrook fired
events.description: The board terminated Easterbrook over a consensual relationship with an employee, and later sued to claw back his severance.

events.title: 2-for-1 stock split
events.description: Nike's seventh split, following a long run in its direct-to-consumer business.

events.title: Kaepernick campaign
events.description: Nike made Colin Kaepernick the face of its 30th-anniversary 'Just Do It' campaign. Boycott calls were immediate; sales rose.

events.title: John Donahoe becomes CEO
events.description: An outsider from eBay and ServiceNow took over to accelerate the shift to direct digital sales, later blamed for weakening wholesale relationships.

events.title: Elliott Hill becomes CEO
events.description: Nike recalled a 32-year company veteran out of retirement to repair retail partnerships and the innovation pipeline.

events.title: Howard Schultz returns as CEO
events.description: Schultz came back after eight years as the financial crisis and over-expansion hit sales, closing 600 US stores and shutting every store for retraining.

events.title: Kevin Johnson becomes CEO
events.description: Schultz moved to executive chairman, handing operations to a technology executive focused on digital ordering.

events.title: Philadelphia arrests and store closures
events.description: The arrest of two Black men waiting in a store led Starbucks to close 8,000 US locations for a day of racial-bias training.

events.title: Schultz returns for a third time
events.description: Schultz came back as interim CEO amid a fast-spreading unionization campaign, and suspended the buyback program on his first day.

events.title: Brian Niccol hired as CEO
events.description: Starbucks poached Chipotle's chief executive; the announcement produced one of the largest single-day gains in the company's history.

events.title: Bank One merger closes
events.description: The $58bn deal brought Jamie Dimon to JPMorgan as president, with a succession agreement making him CEO within two years.

events.title: Bear Stearns rescue
events.description: JPMorgan agreed to buy Bear Stearns for $2 a share — later raised to $10 — with $30bn of Federal Reserve support against its assets.

events.title: Washington Mutual acquired
events.description: JPMorgan bought the banking operations of the largest bank failure in US history for $1.9bn, hours after the FDIC seized it.

events.title: 'London Whale' losses disclosed
events.description: JPMorgan revealed more than $6bn of losses from concentrated credit derivative positions, after Dimon had called concerns 'a tempest in a teapot'.

events.title: First Republic acquired
events.description: JPMorgan bought the failed bank from the FDIC during the regional banking crisis, adding roughly $173bn of loans.

events.title: Visa goes public
events.description: A $17.9bn raise, the largest US IPO to that point, executed weeks after Bear Stearns collapsed.
events.source: Visa Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001403161

events.title: 4-for-1 stock split
events.description: Visa's first split as a public company.

events.title: Visa Europe acquired
events.description: €18.25bn reunited Visa's European member-owned association with the listed company, completing a single global network.

events.title: Plaid acquisition abandoned
events.description: Visa dropped its $5.3bn purchase of the bank-data company after the DOJ sued, alleging it was buying a nascent competitor.

events.title: Mastercard goes public
events.description: Priced at $39 in a conversion from a bank-owned association to a public company — one of the best-performing IPOs of the era.
events.source: Mastercard Inc. Form S-1, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001141391

events.title: 10-for-1 stock split
events.description: Mastercard's share price had passed $800 in the eight years since listing.

events.title: MBNA acquisition closes
events.description: $35bn made Bank of America the largest credit card issuer in the United States.
events.source: Bank of America press release, 1 Jan 2006

events.title: Countrywide acquisition closes
events.description: $4bn for the largest US mortgage lender. The legal and writedown costs that followed are commonly estimated above $50bn.
events.source: Bank of America press release, 1 Jul 2008

events.title: Merrill Lynch acquisition closes
events.description: Agreed over the weekend Lehman failed. Merrill's fourth-quarter losses forced a second federal rescue of Bank of America weeks later.
events.source: Bank of America press release, 1 Jan 2009

events.title: Brian Moynihan becomes CEO
events.description: Moynihan took over from Ken Lewis and spent most of a decade resolving crisis-era litigation.

events.title: $16.65bn DOJ settlement
events.description: The largest civil settlement with a single company in US history, resolving mortgage-securities claims mostly inherited from Countrywide and Merrill.

events.title: Wachovia acquisition closes
events.description: Wells Fargo outbid Citigroup for a bank days from failure, nearly doubling in size and becoming a coast-to-coast franchise.

events.title: Fake accounts scandal breaks
events.description: Regulators fined Wells Fargo $185m after employees opened millions of unauthorized accounts to hit sales targets. The reputational damage far exceeded the fine.

events.title: John Stumpf resigns
events.description: The CEO stepped down and forfeited roughly $69m after two hostile congressional hearings.

events.title: Federal Reserve caps asset growth
events.description: An unprecedented sanction froze Wells Fargo's balance sheet at 2017 levels until governance was fixed, capping earnings for seven years.

events.title: Charlie Scharf becomes CEO
events.description: An outsider from BNY Mellon took over with a mandate to satisfy regulators and lift the asset cap.

events.title: Asset cap lifted
events.description: The Federal Reserve removed the growth restriction after seven years, freeing Wells Fargo to expand its balance sheet again.

events.title: Goldman Sachs goes public
events.description: Priced at $53 after 130 years as a private partnership, ending the last major holdout of the partnership model on Wall Street.
events.source: Goldman Sachs Group Inc. Form S-1, 1999

events.title: Becomes a bank holding company
events.description: Goldman and Morgan Stanley converted overnight to gain Federal Reserve access, ending the independent investment bank as a category.

events.title: $550m SEC settlement
events.description: Goldman settled fraud charges over the Abacus CDO, then the largest penalty ever paid by a Wall Street firm.

events.title: David Solomon becomes CEO
events.description: Solomon succeeded Lloyd Blankfein and pushed into consumer banking, a strategy largely reversed within five years.

events.title: $2.9bn 1MDB settlement
events.description: Goldman's Malaysian subsidiary pleaded guilty in the largest foreign-bribery resolution in DOJ history, and the firm clawed back executive pay.

events.title: Class B shares created
events.description: Buffett issued a lower-priced share class reluctantly, to head off trusts marketing fractional exposure to Berkshire at high fees.

events.title: 50-for-1 Class B split
events.description: Berkshire's only stock split, done so smaller BNSF shareholders could accept stock in the acquisition without tax friction.

events.title: BNSF acquired; joins the S&P 500
events.description: Buffett's largest deal at $34bn — an 'all-in wager on the economic future of the United States'. The split made Berkshire liquid enough for index inclusion the same week.

events.title: Greg Abel named successor
events.description: Charlie Munger disclosed at the annual meeting that Abel would succeed Buffett, resolving the longest-running succession question in US business.

events.title: Buffett announces retirement
events.description: Buffett told shareholders he would step down as CEO at the end of 2025 after 60 years, with Abel taking over.

events.title: CEO resigns over backdating
events.description: William McGuire left amid an options-backdating investigation and returned more than $600m, one of the largest executive repayments ever.

events.title: Change Healthcare acquisition closes
events.description: $13bn after UnitedHealth defeated a DOJ antitrust challenge, consolidating a large share of US claims processing.

events.title: Change Healthcare cyberattack
events.description: A ransomware attack halted claims and payments across the US health system for weeks, and exposed data on roughly 190 million people.

events.title: UnitedHealthcare CEO killed
events.description: Brian Thompson was shot in Manhattan, prompting an unusually hostile public reaction to health insurers and increased political scrutiny.

events.title: Guidance cut on care costs
events.description: UnitedHealth cut full-year guidance on unexpectedly high Medicare Advantage utilization, producing its worst single-day decline in decades.

events.title: Actelion acquisition closes
events.description: $30bn for the Swiss biotech, J&J's largest deal, adding a pulmonary hypertension franchise.

events.title: Talc reporting
events.description: A Reuters investigation reported that J&J had known for decades of asbestos traces in talc, triggering the largest one-day fall in the stock in 16 years.

events.title: Kenvue separation completes
events.description: J&J spun off its consumer brands — Tylenol, Band-Aid, Listerine — to focus on pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

events.title: Mounjaro approved
events.description: FDA approval for type 2 diabetes of a drug whose weight-loss results reset expectations for the entire obesity market.

events.title: Zepbound approved for obesity
events.description: Approval specifically for weight management opened a market analysts sized in the tens of billions, and drove Lilly past every other healthcare company by value.

events.title: Morphic acquisition
events.description: $3.2bn for oral integrin therapies, part of a run of deals funded by incretin cash flows.

events.title: Pharmacia acquisition closes
events.description: $60bn brought Celebrex and made Pfizer the largest pharmaceutical company in the world.

events.title: Wyeth acquisition closes
events.description: $68bn, financed partly through the crisis credit markets, adding vaccines and biologics as Lipitor's patent cliff approached.

events.title: COVID vaccine efficacy announced
events.description: Pfizer and BioNTech reported over 90% efficacy. The news moved the entire market — reopening stocks surged and stay-at-home names fell hard the same session.

events.title: Upjohn spun into Viatris
events.description: Pfizer separated its off-patent business, reshaping itself into a pure research-driven pharmaceutical company.

events.title: Seagen acquisition closes
events.description: $43bn for antibody-drug conjugates, funded by pandemic profits as COVID revenue collapsed.

events.title: Spun off from Abbott
events.description: AbbVie began trading as a separate research pharmaceutical company built around Humira, then heading toward being the best-selling drug in the world.

events.title: Pharmacyclics acquisition closes
events.description: $21bn for Imbruvica, AbbVie's first large move to reduce Humira dependence.

events.title: Allergan acquisition closes
events.description: $63bn added Botox and aesthetics ahead of Humira's US patent expiry.

events.title: Humira biosimilars arrive in the US
events.description: The patent cliff AbbVie had spent a decade preparing for finally hit its largest product.

events.title: Vioxx withdrawn worldwide
events.description: Merck pulled its $2.5bn arthritis drug over cardiovascular risk, wiping roughly a quarter off the share price in a session and beginning years of litigation settled for $4.85bn.

events.title: Schering-Plough merger closes
events.description: $41bn, structured as a reverse merger for tax reasons, adding the biologics pipeline that later included Keytruda.

events.title: Keytruda approved
events.description: The first PD-1 inhibitor approved in the US went on to become the best-selling drug in the world.

events.title: Organon spun off
events.description: Merck separated women's health and legacy brands to concentrate on oncology and vaccines.

events.title: Doug McMillon becomes CEO
events.description: A former hourly associate took over and committed to wage increases and e-commerce investment, compressing margins to defend against Amazon.

events.title: Guidance cut on wage and digital spend
events.description: Walmart warned profits would fall for years while it invested in wages and e-commerce, producing its worst single-day decline in over 25 years.

events.title: Jet.com acquisition closes
events.description: $3.3bn bought e-commerce leadership as much as technology, and Marc Lore went on to run Walmart's US online business.

events.title: Flipkart acquisition closes
events.description: $16bn for 77% of India's largest online retailer, Walmart's biggest deal ever.

events.title: 3-for-1 stock split
events.description: Walmart's first split in 25 years, framed explicitly as making shares accessible to its own associates.

events.title: $7 special dividend
events.description: Costco borrowed $3.5bn to pay a special dividend ahead of an expected tax increase — the first of several that became a signature of its capital policy.

events.title: Amazon buys Whole Foods
events.description: Costco fell sharply on a deal it was not party to, as the market repriced every grocery retailer against Amazon.

events.title: $15 special dividend
events.description: Roughly $6.7bn returned in a single payment, Costco's largest special dividend to date.

events.title: Gillette acquisition closes
events.description: $57bn, P&G's largest deal, adding razors and batteries and making it the largest consumer goods company in the world.

events.title: Plan to shed ~100 brands
events.description: P&G announced it would divest more than half its brands to concentrate on the 70-80 that generated nearly all its profit.

events.title: Peltz proxy fight
events.description: The most expensive proxy contest in corporate history ended in a near-tie; Nelson Peltz joined the board months later.

events.title: North American bottling acquired
events.description: Coca-Cola took its largest bottler back in-house for $12.3bn, reversing a two-decade refranchising strategy it would later reverse again.

events.title: 2-for-1 stock split
events.description: Coca-Cola's eleventh split since 1927.

events.title: James Quincey becomes CEO
events.description: Quincey accelerated the move beyond carbonated soft drinks into water, coffee and smaller pack sizes.

events.title: Costa Coffee acquisition closes
events.description: $4.9bn bought a global coffee chain, Coca-Cola's clearest push outside packaged drinks.

events.title: Quaker Oats acquisition closes
events.description: $13.4bn was really a purchase of Gatorade, which became one of the best returns on capital in consumer goods.

events.title: Indra Nooyi becomes CEO
events.description: Nooyi reoriented PepsiCo toward 'performance with purpose' and a healthier product mix, drawing activist pressure over slower soda growth.

events.title: Bottlers brought back in-house
events.description: PepsiCo acquired its two largest bottlers for $7.8bn, taking direct control of distribution.

events.title: Ramon Laguarta becomes CEO
events.description: A 22-year company veteran took over and shifted capital toward snacks, which by then out-earned beverages.

events.title: XTO Energy acquisition closes
events.description: $41bn bet on US natural gas, made near a price peak. Exxon wrote down much of the value over the following decade.

events.title: Removed from the Dow Jones
events.description: Exxon was dropped after 92 years — the longest-running member — and replaced by Salesforce, marking the index's rotation out of energy.
events.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices announcement, 24 Aug 2020

events.title: Engine No. 1 wins board seats
events.description: A hedge fund holding roughly 0.02% of Exxon won three board seats on a climate platform, one of the most striking activist results ever.

events.title: Pioneer acquisition closes
events.description: $60bn, Exxon's largest deal since the Mobil merger, roughly doubling its Permian Basin production.

events.title: Texaco merger completes
events.description: $45bn created ChevronTexaco, the second-largest US oil company.

events.title: Unocal acquisition closes
events.description: $18bn after Chevron outbid CNOOC in a contest that became a US political fight over Chinese ownership of energy assets.

events.title: Noble Energy acquisition closes
events.description: $5bn in stock, bought cheaply during the pandemic oil collapse.

events.title: Hess acquisition closes
events.description: $53bn completed after Chevron won an arbitration against Exxon over Guyana rights, adding one of the largest oil discoveries in decades.

events.title: Bucyrus acquisition closes
events.description: $8.8bn for mining equipment at the top of the commodity supercycle; demand fell sharply within two years.

events.title: Siwei fraud writedown
events.description: Caterpillar took a $580m charge after discovering accounting misconduct at a Chinese subsidiary acquired months earlier.

events.title: Federal agents search facilities
events.description: IRS and other federal agents executed warrants at three Illinois facilities in a tax investigation, and the stock fell sharply intraday.

events.title: First 787 delivered
events.description: The Dreamliner entered service more than three years late, after an outsourced supply chain proved far harder to integrate than planned.

events.title: Lion Air Flight 610 crashes
events.description: 189 people died. Investigators identified MCAS, flight-control software pilots had not been told about.

events.title: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashes
events.description: 157 people died in a second 737 MAX accident with the same signature five months after the first.

events.title: 737 MAX grounded worldwide
events.description: The FAA grounded the fleet after most other regulators had already done so — the longest grounding of a US airliner in history, at 20 months.

events.title: 737 MAX ungrounded
events.description: The FAA cleared the aircraft to fly after design changes and new pilot training requirements.

events.title: Alaska Airlines door plug blows out
events.description: A panel departed a nearly new 737 MAX 9 in flight. The FAA capped Boeing's production rate, and the quality crisis cost the CEO his job.

events.title: Kelly Ortberg becomes CEO
events.description: An aerospace outsider took over and moved the CEO's office to Seattle, closer to manufacturing.

events.title: 33,000 workers strike
events.description: Boeing's first strike since 2008 halted most commercial production for seven weeks and forced a large equity raise.

events.title: Jeff Immelt becomes CEO
events.description: Immelt succeeded Jack Welch four days before September 11. GE lost roughly 30% of its value over his 16-year tenure.

events.title: Dividend cut 68%
events.description: GE cut a dividend it had not reduced since the Great Depression, as GE Capital's funding model failed in the credit crisis.

events.title: Dividend halved again
events.description: New CEO John Flannery cut the dividend a second time and disclosed the scale of the industrial cash shortfall.

events.title: Removed from the Dow Jones
events.description: GE was dropped after 111 years — the last original member of the 1896 index still present.
events.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices announcement, 19 Jun 2018

events.title: Larry Culp becomes CEO
events.description: The first outsider to run GE took over with the stock near a 20-year low, and began selling businesses to repair the balance sheet.

events.title: 1-for-8 reverse split
events.description: GE reduced its share count to reflect a company a fraction of its former size after years of divestitures.

events.title: Three-way split completes
events.description: GE finished separating into GE Aerospace, GE HealthCare and GE Vernova, ending the conglomerate model Jack Welch had made famous.

events.title: UPS goes public
events.description: A $5.47bn raise, the largest US IPO to that point, after 92 years of employee and family ownership.
events.source: United Parcel Service Inc. Form S-1, 1999

events.title: Carol Tomé becomes CEO
events.description: The first outsider to lead UPS took over during the pandemic e-commerce surge with a 'better not bigger' strategy.

events.title: Teamsters contract ratified
events.description: A five-year agreement averted a strike but raised labour costs sharply, and the threat alone had diverted volume to competitors.

events.title: Amazon volume to be halved
events.description: UPS said it would cut deliveries for its largest customer by more than 50%, choosing margin over volume; the stock fell sharply.
